notes.NC17.2.OA.1: All amounts and answers are within 100. Skills: one-step result unknown (4), put together (5), change unknown (2), start unknown (3), compare (5), matching to an equation (4), two-step (7, including start-unknown and change-unknown ones). All numbers and results are within 100. Unknowns in every position, add-to/take-from/put-together/compare, one- and two-step, and matching stories to equations.
notes.NC17.2.OA.2: Two-addend facts within 20 only (no three-addend sums); all numbers and results stay within 20.
notes.NC17.2.OA.3: Odd/even answers are words, so those are choice questions; numeric ones ask for pairs, leftovers, group sizes or the number in a doubles equation. All numbers stay within 20.
notes.NC17.2.OA.4: Arrays are described in words (rows and columns) and total at most 25 (5 by 5). Where a sum is asked, options never include the column-wise sum of the same array, so exactly one option is correct. Arrays kept within 5 by 5; sums of arrays put together may total more than 25. All stems are stories or written-out arrays.
notes.NC17.2.NBT.2: Whole numbers within 1000 only; no counting back by 5s, 10s or 100s (the standard names skip-counting forward). Skills: count on by ones (3), count back by ones (3), skip-count by 10s (6), by 5s (5), by 100s (6), missing number in a pattern (4), rule of a pattern (3).
notes.NC17.2.NBT.3: All numbers are below 1000 (a few two-digit ones at difficulty 1). Number words are written with hyphens, e.g. forty-six. Numerals and expanded forms are asked both ways; a words answer is a choice question. Expanded-form distractors never include a valid sum (e.g. 400 + 18 for 418) so only one option is correct.
notes.NC17.2.NBT.4: Statements of comparison are written with the symbols in $...$. Answers are whole numbers or a digit; a symbol alone is never an option (only three symbols exist), so the symbol is chosen inside a full statement.
notes.NC17.2.NBT.6: Sums stay under 300 (three two-digit numbers at most). Missing-addend questions are solved by counting up or knowing the sum, not by formal subtraction rules. Place-value drawings are replaced by tens-and-ones sentences.
notes.NC17.2.NBT.7: Within 1000, whole numbers only. Written methods are described in words rather than shown as columns.
notes.NC17.2.NBT.8: Starting numbers are kept between 100 and 900 as the standard says; answers stay within 1,000.
notes.NC17.2.MD.1: All 30 written in words only (no pictures of rulers): readings are given as marks (start/end). Tool choice, unit choice and reading/subtracting from a ruler are covered; 19 choice and 11 numeric because tool and unit questions are naturally choice. Conversions between units (MD.2) and estimating (MD.3) deliberately left out.
notes.NC17.2.MD.3: Grade 2 estimation of length is tested with reasonable-length choices, best-unit choices, and estimates built from a stated benchmark length (a hand, a paper clip, a step). No conversions between units are asked (those belong to later grades); comparing units asks only that a longer unit takes a smaller count.
notes.NC17.2.MD.4: Lengths are given in words and as ruler marks; no picture is needed.
notes.NC17.2.MD.5: Whole-number lengths within 100 (inches, feet, centimeters, meters), no units in numeric answers. Skills: add lengths to a total (5), subtract for the length left (5), compare two lengths (6), unknown part or start (6), choose the equation with a ? (5), two-step (3). Every equation question has one equation that fits; the others each come from a mix-up of the operation or of the places of the numbers.
notes.NC17.2.MD.6: Number lines are described in words (start, jump left or right, land on). Skills: show a whole number as a length from 0 (5), add on a number line (8), subtract on a number line (6), match jumps to a number sentence (6), find the distance between two points (5). All numbers within 100. Missing-jump questions are phrased as the length of a jump between two points on the line, as the standard asks for differences on it.
notes.NC17.2.MD.7: Grade 2: clocks are described by where the short and long hand point, since no picture is shown; times are plain text such as 3:20 p.m. A time cannot be a numeric answer, so questions whose answer is a time are choice questions, and numeric ones ask for the minutes, the hand's number or one part of the time (10 numeric, 20 choice). The nearest-five-minutes skill is asked with the hand a little before or a little past a number, and with a digital time. Elapsed time is left out.
notes.NC17.2.MD.8: Grade 2: the cent and dollar symbols are written as words ("cents", "dollars"), because the bank allows no dollar sign; the cent sign is avoided too. Amounts are all in cents (under 100) or all in whole dollars, never mixed. Coin pictures are described by coin names.
notes.NC17.2.MD.10: Graphs are written out as lists of counts (each picture stands for 1, bars go up by ones); building a graph is tested as the number of pictures or the height of a bar, not by drawing. Numbers stay within 35 except totals.
notes.NC17.2.G.1: Drawing is asked as naming or counting what would be drawn, since the questions are text only. Trapezoids and rhombuses are left out as they belong to later grades; vertices are always glossed as corners.
notes.NC17.2.G.3: Circles and rectangles are described in words; no pictures. "Equal shares can differ in shape" is asked from written cutting descriptions.

solve.work: 6 ft: 12-in ruler needs 6 moves, yardstick 2, meter stick ~2; 10-foot tape does it in one.

questions.skill: Read a length from the 0 mark
questions.stem: Jun lines a stick up at 0 on a meter stick. The stick ends at the 64 centimeter mark. A second stick is 9 centimeters longer than the first. How many centimeters long is the second stick?
questions.solution: The first stick starts at 0 and ends at 64, so it is 64 centimeters long. The second stick is 9 centimeters longer: 64 + 9 = 73.

questions.skill: Find a length that starts at a mark other than 0
questions.stem: A board starts at the 15 inch mark of a yardstick and ends at the 33 inch mark. How many inches long is the board?
questions.solution: The board starts at 15, not at 0. Subtract: 33 - 15 = 18. The board is 18 inches long.

questions.skill: Find a length that starts at a mark other than 0
questions.stem: A rope is laid along a tape measure. One end is at the 71 centimeter mark and the other end is at the 26 centimeter mark. How many centimeters long is the rope?
questions.solution: The rope runs between the 26 mark and the 71 mark. Subtract the smaller number from the larger: 71 - 26 = 45. The rope is 45 centimeters long.

questions.skill: Choose a unit of length that fits
questions.stem: A classroom door is about 7 ___ tall. Which unit makes the sentence sensible?
questions.solution: A door is taller than a person. 7 feet fits. 7 inches or 7 centimeters would be shorter than a pencil, and 7 miles is far too long.

solve.work: A door is about 7 feet tall (about 2 m); 7 inches/centimeters too small, miles absurd.

questions.skill: Use a measuring tool the right way
questions.stem: Rae measures a pencil. It starts at the 2 inch mark and ends at the 9 inch mark. She says it is 9 inches long. What should she have done?
choices: She should have added 2 and 9, so it is 11 inches long.
She should have subtracted 2 from 9, so it is 7 inches long.
She should have used the 2, so it is 2 inches long.
She is right, because the end mark is 9, so it is 9 inches long.
questions.answer: She should have subtracted 2 from 9, so it is 7 inches long.
questions.solution: The pencil starts at 2, not 0, so the end mark is not its length. Subtract: 9 - 2 = 7. The pencil is 7 inches long.

solve.answer: She should have subtracted 2 from 9, so it is 7 inches long.
solve.work: Length = 9 - 2 = 7 inches; she should have subtracted.

questions.skill: Use a measuring tool the right way
questions.stem: Dan uses a broken ruler that starts at the 3 centimeter mark. He lines one end of a straw up with the first mark on the broken ruler, which says 3. The other end of the straw is at the 15 centimeter mark. How many centimeters long is the straw?
questions.solution: The straw starts at 3, not 0. Subtract: 15 - 3 = 12. The straw is 12 centimeters long.

questions.skill: Know which units a measuring tool shows
questions.stem: Which of these lengths would you read from a meter stick?
questions.solution: A meter stick is marked in centimeters, so 58 centimeters can be read from it. A meter stick has no inches, and pounds and cups are not lengths.

solve.work: A meter stick is marked in centimeters; pounds and cups are not lengths.

questions.skill: Know which units a measuring tool shows

choices: either edge, since the numbers are the same
the biggest number on the tape
questions.solution: Jo wants centimeters, so she reads the edge marked in centimeters. The two edges give different numbers because inches and centimeters are different sizes.

solve.work: Read the edge marked in centimeters.

questions.skill: Predict which measurement is the larger number
questions.stem: Mia measures a table in feet and then in inches. Which measurement is the larger number?
questions.solution: An inch is shorter than a foot, so it takes more inches than feet to cover the same table. The number of inches is the larger number.

solve.work: An inch is shorter than a foot, so more inches fit along the table: the number of inches is larger.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit

questions.solution: Each of the 2 yards is 3 feet: 3 + 3 = 6. The rope is 6 feet long.

questions.skill: Tell which unit is longer from two measurements
questions.stem: A mat is 3 yards long. It is also 9 feet long. Which unit is longer?
questions.solution: The same mat needs only 3 yards but 9 feet. The longer the unit, the fewer you need, so a yard is longer than a foot.

solve.work: 3 yards = 9 feet, so it takes fewer yards: a yard is the longer unit (1 yard = 3 feet).

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit

questions.solution: Two meters is 100 + 100 = 200 centimeters.

questions.skill: Explain why the numbers differ using unit size

An inch is longer than a foot, so measuring in inches gives a bigger number.
An inch is the same as a foot, so both give the same number.

questions.skill: Compare two measurements of one object

questions.solution: 12 - 4 = 8. He counted 8 more feet than yards because a foot is shorter than a yard.

questions.skill: Predict which measurement is the larger number
questions.stem: Dan will measure his bed with a yardstick and then with a 1-foot ruler. Which will he need more of?
choices: He needs the same number of each
questions.solution: A foot is shorter than a yard, so more 1-foot rulers than yardsticks will fit along the bed.

solve.work: A foot ruler is shorter than a yardstick, so he must lay it down more times.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A towel is 2 feet long. Each foot is 12 inches long. How many inches long is the towel?
questions.solution: Two feet is 12 + 12 = 24 inches.

questions.skill: Tell which unit is longer from two measurements
questions.stem: A pole is 5 meters long. It is also 500 centimeters long. Which unit is shorter?
questions.solution: The pole is 500 centimeters but only 5 meters. It takes more of the shorter unit, so a centimeter is shorter than a meter.

solve.work: 500 centimeters vs 5 meters: more centimeters, so a centimeter is the shorter unit.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit

questions.solution: 6 feet is two groups of 3 feet. So the rope is 2 yards long.

questions.skill: Explain why the numbers differ using unit size

choices: A foot is longer than a yard, so it takes more feet.
A foot is shorter than a yard, so it takes fewer feet.
One of them measured the sandbox wrong.
A foot is shorter than a yard, so it takes more feet.

solve.answer: A foot is shorter than a yard, so it takes more feet.
solve.work: A foot is shorter than a yard, so more feet are needed: 12 feet vs 4 yards.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A tunnel is 5 meters long. Each meter is 100 centimeters long. How many centimeters long is the tunnel?
questions.solution: Five meters is 5 groups of 100 centimeters: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A rope is 15 feet long. Every 3 feet make 1 yard. How many yards long is the rope?
questions.solution: Count by threes to 15: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. That is 5 groups, so the rope is 5 yards long.

questions.skill: Tell which unit is longer from two measurements
questions.stem: A desk is 2 meters long. It is also 200 centimeters long. Which statement is true?
choices: The desk has fewer meters than centimeters because a meter is longer.
The desk has fewer meters than centimeters because a meter is shorter.
The desk has more meters than centimeters because a meter is longer.
The desk has the same number of meters and centimeters.
questions.answer: The desk has fewer meters than centimeters because a meter is longer.
questions.solution: A meter is a longer unit, so fewer meters are needed to cover the desk than centimeters.

solve.answer: The desk has fewer meters than centimeters because a meter is longer.
solve.work: 2 meters vs 200 centimeters: fewer meters, because a meter is the longer unit.

questions.skill: Predict which measurement is the larger number

questions.solution: A yard is longer than a foot, so fewer yards than feet are needed. Her new number will be less than 36.

solve.work: A yard is longer than a foot, so the number in yards is smaller than 36 (it is 12).

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A pencil is 12 centimeters long. Each paper clip is 3 centimeters long. How many paper clips, laid end to end with no gaps, are as long as the pencil?
questions.solution: Count by threes to 12: 3, 6, 9, 12. That is 4 paper clips.

questions.skill: Explain why the numbers differ using unit size
questions.stem: Max measured a rope with a 1-foot ruler and got 6. Then he measured it with a yardstick and got 2. Why is 2 the smaller number?
choices: A yard is shorter than a foot, so fewer yardsticks fit along the rope.
A yard is longer than a foot, so more yardsticks fit along the rope.
A yard is longer than a foot, so fewer yardsticks fit along the rope.
The rope got shorter when he measured it the second time.
questions.answer: A yard is longer than a foot, so fewer yardsticks fit along the rope.
questions.solution: The rope did not change. A yardstick is longer than a 1-foot ruler, so fewer of them are needed.

solve.answer: A yard is longer than a foot, so fewer yardsticks fit along the rope.
solve.work: A yard is longer than a foot, so fewer yardsticks fit: 2 vs 6.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A sofa is 2 yards long. Each yard is 36 inches long. How many inches long is the sofa?
questions.solution: Two yards is 36 + 36 = 72 inches.

questions.skill: Tell which unit is longer from two measurements
questions.stem: Pia says her kite string is 5 meters long. Leo says the same string is 500 centimeters long. Both are right. Which unit is longer?
questions.solution: The same string is 5 meters or 500 centimeters. Fewer meters are needed, so a meter is the longer unit.

solve.work: 5 meters = 500 cm: fewer meters, so a meter is longer.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A rope is 2 yards long. Each yard is 3 feet long. Which is the same length as the rope?
questions.solution: Two yards is 3 + 3 = 6 feet. Adding 2 and 3 gives 5, which is not the same.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A rope is 5 yards long. Jon cuts off 2 yards. How many feet long is the piece that is left? (Each yard is 3 feet.)
questions.solution: The piece left is 5 - 2 = 3 yards. Three yards is 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 feet.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A cord is 36 inches long. Ava cuts it into pieces that are each 1 foot long. How many pieces does she get? (Each foot is 12 inches.)
questions.solution: Count by twelves to 36: 12, 24, 36. That is 3 pieces.

questions.skill: Explain why the numbers differ using unit size
questions.stem: Ana measured a window with Tool 1 and got 24. Ben measured the same window with Tool 2 and got 8. Which statement is true?
choices: The unit of Tool 2 is shorter than the unit of Tool 1.
The unit of Tool 2 is longer than the unit of Tool 1.
The units of both tools are the same length.
The window is longer in Ana's measurement.
questions.answer: The unit of Tool 2 is longer than the unit of Tool 1.
questions.solution: Ben needed fewer units to cover the same window, so his unit is longer.

solve.answer: The unit of Tool 2 is longer than the unit of Tool 1.
solve.work: Same window, Tool 2 gives the smaller count (8 < 24), so its unit is longer.

questions.skill: Compare two measurements of one object
questions.stem: A table is 24 inches long. Ana lays 6-inch blocks along it, end to end. Ben lays 4-inch blocks along it. How many more blocks does Ben use than Ana?
questions.solution: Ana uses 24 / 6 = 4 blocks. Ben uses 24 / 4 = 6 blocks. 6 - 4 = 2, so Ben uses 2 more blocks.

questions.skill: Predict which measurement is the larger number
questions.stem: A rope is measured three ways: in inches, in feet and in yards. Which list gives the units in order from the smallest number to the largest number?
questions.solution: The longest unit gives the smallest number. A yard is longer than a foot, and a foot is longer than an inch. So the order is yards, feet, inches.

solve.work: The longest unit gives the smallest number: yards (smallest number), then feet, then inches (largest number).

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A path is 3 meters long. Jo walks 1 meter of it. How many centimeters of the path are left? (Each meter is 100 centimeters.)
questions.solution: The part left is 3 - 1 = 2 meters. Two meters is 200 centimeters.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: Which pair of measurements could be for the same board? (Each foot is 12 inches.)
questions.solution: Two feet is 12 + 12 = 24 inches. So only 2 feet and 24 inches match.

solve.work: 2 feet = 12 + 12 = 24 inches. So 2 feet and 24 inches.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: A ribbon is 3 yards long. A string is 6 feet long. How many feet long are the two together? (Each yard is 3 feet.)
questions.solution: The ribbon is 3 yards = 9 feet. Add the string: 9 + 6 = 15 feet.

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: Sam measured a fence and got 7 yards. What is the length of the same fence in feet? (Each yard is 3 feet.)
questions.solution: Seven yards of 3 feet each is 7 x 3 = 21 feet. The other numbers come from subtracting, adding or doubling.

solve.work: 7 yards = 7 x 3 = 21 feet (count by 3s seven times).

questions.skill: Find the measurement in a second unit
questions.stem: Lia measured a flagpole with a meter stick and got 4. Mei measured the same flagpole with 1-centimeter cubes. How many cubes did Mei use? (Each meter is 100 centimeters.)
questions.solution: Four meters is 4 groups of 100 centimeters, which is 400 centimeters. So Mei used 400 cubes.

questions.skill: Choose a reasonable length for an object
questions.stem: Which is the most reasonable length for a new pencil?
questions.solution: A new pencil is about as long as a hand, so 7 inches is about right. 7 feet is taller than a door, and 7 yards and 7 meters are even longer.

solve.work: A new pencil is about 7 inches (about 19 cm). 7 feet, yards or meters are far too long.

questions.skill: Choose the best unit for measuring a length
questions.stem: Which unit is best for measuring how long a bean is?
questions.solution: A bean is very small. An inch is a small unit, so inches fit best. A foot, a yard and a meter are much too long for a bean.

solve.work: A bean is a few centimeters / about 1 inch long; inches is the smallest unit offered.

questions.skill: Estimate a length by repeating a known length
questions.stem: Maya's shoe is about 1 foot long. She lays it end to end along a rug, and it fits 6 times. About how many feet long is the rug?
questions.solution: Each time the shoe fits, that is about 1 foot. 6 shoes is about 6 feet, so the rug is about 6 feet long.

solve.work: Shoe about 1 foot, fits 6 times: 6 x 1 = 6 feet.

questions.skill: Compare lengths and the size of different units
questions.stem: Which is the longest length?
questions.solution: All four use the number 5, so compare the units. A yard is longer than a foot, an inch or a centimeter, so 5 yards is the longest.

solve.work: Centimeter < inch < foot < yard, so 5 yards is longest.

questions.skill: Judge an estimate of a length
questions.stem: Ben says his thumb is about 2 feet long. What is a better estimate for the length of his thumb?
questions.solution: A thumb is short. 2 feet is longer than a ruler, so it is too long. 2 inches is about right. 2 yards, 2 meters and 20 feet are even longer.

solve.work: A thumb is about 2 inches long; 2 feet, 20 feet, 2 yards, 2 meters are all far too long.

questions.skill: Choose a reasonable length for an object
questions.stem: A school bus is parked at the curb. Which is the most reasonable length for it?
questions.solution: A school bus is very long. 10 centimeters and 10 inches are shorter than a ruler, and 10 feet is shorter than a car. 10 meters is the best estimate.

solve.work: A school bus is about 35-40 feet, about 10-12 meters. 10 feet is too short, 10 cm/10 in tiny.

questions.skill: Estimate a length by repeating a known length
questions.stem: A hand is about 10 centimeters wide. A book is as long as 3 hands side by side. About how many centimeters long is the book?
questions.solution: The book is about 3 hands long and each hand is about 10 centimeters. 10 + 10 + 10 = 30, so the book is about 30 centimeters long.

questions.skill: Choose a reasonable length for an object

solve.work: A soup spoon is about 15-18 cm. 2 cm too small, 150 cm and 1,500 cm far too big.

questions.skill: Choose the best unit for measuring a length

questions.solution: A pencil case is small, so a small unit is best. A centimeter is small. A yard, a meter and a foot are all too long to be handy for a pencil case.

solve.work: A pencil case is about 20 cm, less than a foot; centimeters is the best of the units offered.

He gets the same number both ways.
He gets a smaller number in yards than in feet.
The hallway gets longer when he uses yards.

solve.work: A kitchen table is about 30 inches tall (about 76 cm). 30 cm is about 1 foot, too low; 30 ft/yd far too tall.

questions.skill: Estimate one length from another
questions.stem: A door is about 2 meters tall. A bed is about as long as that door is tall, and a rug beside the bed is about 1 meter shorter than the bed. About how many meters long is the rug?
questions.solution: The bed is about 2 meters long, the same as the door is tall. The rug is 1 meter shorter, so it is about 2 - 1 = 1 meter long.

solve.work: Door about 2 m, bed about 2 m, rug 1 m shorter: 2 - 1 = 1 m.

questions.skill: Choose the best unit for measuring a length

solve.work: A button is about 1-2 cm; the pool, bus and hallway are measured in meters.

questions.skill: Estimate a length by repeating a known length

questions.solution: Each bench is about 2 yards. 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8, so the row is about 8 yards long.

questions.skill: Compare lengths and the size of different units

solve.work: inch < foot < yard, so 6 inches, 6 feet, 6 yards.

questions.solution: A desk top is longer than a ruler but shorter than a door is tall. About 2 feet fits. 8 feet and 20 yards are far too long, and 8 centimeters is smaller than a pencil.

questions.skill: Estimate one length from another

questions.solution: Half of 100 is 50, so Max's sister is about 50 centimeters tall.

questions.solution: Each giant step is about 1 yard. He takes 12 + 9 = 21 steps in all, so he goes about 21 yards.

questions.skill: Estimate a length by repeating a known length

solve.work: A pencil is about 20 cm and a tall tree about 10 m. The other pairs put a pencil at 20 m or a tree at 10 cm.

questions.stem: Dad draws a pentagon and a hexagon. How many straight sides do the two shapes have in all?
questions.solution: A pentagon has 5 sides and a hexagon has 6 sides. 5 + 6 = 11 sides.

questions.skill: Recognise quadrilaterals (squares and rectangles)
questions.stem: Which shape has 4 straight sides that are all the same length and 4 square corners?
questions.solution: A square has 4 sides of equal length and 4 square corners. A long, thin rectangle has sides of different lengths. A hexagon has 6 sides and a triangle has 3.

solve.work: 4 equal sides and 4 square corners: a square.

questions.skill: Recognise quadrilaterals (squares and rectangles)
questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a quadrilateral?
choices: A shape with 4 sides and 4 corners
A shape with 6 sides and 6 corners
questions.answer: A shape with 6 sides and 6 corners
questions.solution: A quadrilateral has 4 sides. A shape with 6 sides and 6 corners is a hexagon, so it is not a quadrilateral. The squares and rectangles all have 4 sides.

solve.answer: A shape with 6 sides and 6 corners
solve.work: A 6-sided shape is a hexagon, not a quadrilateral; the others have 4 sides.

questions.skill: Describe a cube (faces, edges, vertices)
questions.stem: Jo builds the frame of a cube from straws. She uses 1 straw for each edge. How many straws does she need?
questions.solution: A cube has 12 edges: 4 on the top, 4 on the bottom and 4 going up the sides. She needs 12 straws.

questions.skill: Describe a cube (faces, edges, vertices)
questions.stem: Which sentence is true about every cube?
choices: It has 8 faces that are squares
It has 6 faces that are triangles
It has 12 faces that are squares
It has 6 faces that are squares
questions.answer: It has 6 faces that are squares
questions.solution: A cube has 6 faces, and every face is a square.

solve.answer: It has 6 faces that are squares

questions.skill: Recognise quadrilaterals (squares and rectangles)
questions.stem: Kim has these shapes: triangle, hexagon, square, triangle, pentagon, rectangle, hexagon. How many of them are quadrilaterals?
questions.solution: A quadrilateral has 4 sides. The square and the rectangle each have 4 sides. The other shapes do not. So 2 shapes are quadrilaterals.

questions.skill: Describe a rectangular prism and name solids
questions.stem: Which sentence is true about a rectangular prism?
questions.solution: A rectangular prism has 6 faces and 12 edges (and 8 vertices).

questions.skill: Count the sides or corners of polygons
questions.stem: A shape has 3 fewer sides than a hexagon. How many sides does it have?
questions.solution: A hexagon has 6 sides. 6 - 3 = 3 sides. That shape is a triangle.

questions.skill: Describe a cube (faces, edges, vertices)
questions.stem: Which shape is a face of a cube?
questions.solution: Every face of a cube is a square.

solve.work: A face of a cube is a square.

questions.skill: Count the sides or corners of polygons
questions.stem: Kai wants to draw a shape with more than 4 sides but fewer than 6 sides. How many sides must his shape have?
questions.solution: The only number between 4 and 6 is 5. His shape has 5 sides. It is a pentagon.

questions.skill: Name a polygon from its sides or corners
questions.stem: Which shape has 2 more sides than a quadrilateral?
questions.solution: A quadrilateral has 4 sides. 4 + 2 = 6 sides. A shape with 6 sides is a hexagon.

questions.skill: Count the sides or corners of polygons
questions.stem: Lia has 3 quadrilaterals and 2 hexagons. How many straight sides do her shapes have in all?
questions.solution: The 3 quadrilaterals have 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 sides. The 2 hexagons have 6 + 6 = 12 sides. 12 + 12 = 24 sides.

questions.skill: Describe a rectangular prism and name solids
questions.stem: Which solid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, but its faces are not all the same size?
questions.solution: A cube and a rectangular prism both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. In a cube all the faces are the same size. So the solid is a rectangular prism. A cone and a cylinder have different numbers.

solve.work: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices with faces not all the same size: rectangular prism (a cube has all faces equal).

questions.skill: Describe a cube (faces, edges, vertices)
questions.stem: Max builds a cube from straws and balls of clay. He uses 1 straw for each edge and 1 ball of clay for each vertex. How many pieces does he use in all?
questions.solution: A cube has 12 edges, so 12 straws. It has 8 vertices, so 8 balls of clay. 12 + 8 = 20 pieces.

questions.skill: Recognise quadrilaterals (squares and rectangles)
questions.stem: Which statement is true?
questions.solution: A rectangle has 4 sides, so it is a quadrilateral. A quadrilateral can have sides of different lengths. A hexagon has 6 sides and a triangle has 3 corners.

solve.work: A rectangle has 4 sides, so every rectangle is a quadrilateral; the others are false.

questions.skill: Count the sides or corners of polygons
questions.stem: Pam has 2 triangles, a pentagon and a hexagon. How many corners do her 4 shapes have in all?
questions.solution: A triangle has 3 corners, a pentagon 5 and a hexagon 6. 3 + 3 + 5 + 6 = 17 corners.

questions.skill: Recognise quadrilaterals (squares and rectangles)
questions.stem: A square piece of paper is cut by one straight cut from one corner to the opposite corner. How many sides does each piece have?
questions.solution: The cut goes corner to corner, so each piece is a triangle. A triangle has 3 sides.

solve.work: A diagonal cut gives two triangles, each with 3 sides.

questions.skill: Describe a cube (faces, edges, vertices)
questions.stem: Which statement about a cube is NOT true?
choices: All 6 of its faces are squares of the same size
Some faces are rectangles that are not squares
It has 12 edges, and each edge joins 2 faces
It has 8 vertices, where the edges meet
questions.answer: Some faces are rectangles that are not squares
questions.solution: Every face of a cube is a square, so it has no faces that are rectangles but not squares. The other statements are true.

solve.answer: Some faces are rectangles that are not squares
solve.work: All cube faces are squares, so "some faces are rectangles that are not squares" is false; the others are true.

questions.skill: Describe a rectangular prism and name solids
questions.stem: Kim covers every face of a box shaped like a rectangular prism with paper. She uses 1 sheet for each face. She has 10 sheets. How many sheets are left?
questions.solution: A rectangular prism has 6 faces, so Kim uses 6 sheets. 10 - 6 = 4 sheets are left.

questions.skill: Name a polygon from its sides or corners
questions.stem: A shape has 3 fewer sides than a cube has vertices (corners). Which shape is it?
questions.solution: A cube has 8 vertices. 8 - 3 = 5 sides. A shape with 5 sides is a pentagon.

solve.work: A cube has 8 vertices; 8 - 3 = 5 sides: pentagon.

questions.skill: Name equal shares as halves, thirds or fourths
questions.stem: A pizza is cut into 3 equal shares. What is each share called?
questions.solution: A whole cut into 3 equal shares has thirds. Each share is a third.

questions.skill: Name equal shares as halves, thirds or fourths
questions.stem: Rita cuts a ribbon into 2 equal parts. Each part is what part of the ribbon?
questions.solution: 2 equal parts are halves, so each part is a half of the ribbon.

questions.skill: Name equal shares as halves, thirds or fourths
questions.stem: Which word means the same as a fourth?
questions.solution: A fourth is 1 of 4 equal shares. It is also called a quarter.

questions.skill: Tell equal shares from unequal pieces
questions.stem: Which is a way to cut a circle into thirds?
choices: Into 3 pieces, one much bigger than the others
Into 3 pieces that are the same size
Into 2 pieces that are the same size
Into 4 pieces that are the same size
questions.answer: Into 3 pieces that are the same size
questions.solution: Thirds are 3 EQUAL shares. The 3 pieces must be the same size.

solve.answer: Into 3 pieces that are the same size

questions.skill: Name equal shares as halves, thirds or fourths
questions.stem: Three children share a pie equally. What part of the pie does each child get?
questions.solution: 3 equal shares are thirds. Each child gets a third of the pie.

solve.work: Shared equally among 3: each a third.

questions.skill: Count the equal shares in a whole
questions.stem: A pie is cut into thirds. How many equal shares are there?
questions.solution: Thirds are 3 equal shares.

questions.skill: Count the equal shares in a whole
questions.stem: A garden is cut into halves. How many equal parts is that?
questions.solution: Halves are 2 equal shares.

questions.skill: A whole is made of its shares
questions.stem: How many fourths make 1 whole?
questions.solution: 1 whole cut into fourths has 4 equal shares, so 4 fourths make 1 whole.

questions.skill: Share equally among people
questions.stem: A pizza is cut into thirds. Each friend gets 1 third and there is none left over. How many friends are there?
questions.solution: The pizza has 3 thirds and each friend takes 1, so there are 3 friends.

solve.work: 3 thirds, one per friend, none left: 3 friends.

questions.skill: Share equally among people
questions.stem: Four friends will share a sandwich equally. Into how many equal shares should it be cut?
questions.solution: There are 4 friends, so the sandwich needs 4 equal shares.

questions.skill: Tell equal shares from unequal pieces
questions.stem: To cut a cake into fourths, what must be true about the 4 pieces?
choices: They are all the same size
They are all the same shape
They are all a different color
questions.answer: They are all the same size
questions.solution: Fourths are equal shares, so the pieces must be the same size. (Equal shares can still be different shapes.)

solve.answer: They are all the same size
solve.work: Fourths must be equal in size; they need not be the same shape.

questions.skill: A whole is made of its shares
questions.stem: Which makes 1 whole pizza?
questions.solution: A pizza cut into 3 equal shares has 3 thirds. All 3 thirds together make the whole pizza.

solve.work: 3 thirds make 1 whole; 3 fourths, 2 thirds, 1 half do not.

questions.skill: More equal shares make smaller shares
questions.stem: Two pizzas are the same size. One is cut into thirds and the other into fourths. Which sentence is true?
choices: A fourth is bigger than a third
A third is bigger than a fourth
A third and a fourth are the same size
It cannot be told which is bigger
questions.answer: A third is bigger than a fourth
questions.solution: The pizza cut into 3 shares has fewer, bigger shares than the pizza cut into 4. So a third is bigger than a fourth.

solve.answer: A third is bigger than a fourth
solve.work: Fewer shares are bigger: a third is bigger than a fourth.

questions.skill: Tell equal shares from unequal pieces
questions.stem: Lena cuts a pancake into 3 pieces. Two pieces are small and the same size. The third piece is much bigger. Are these pieces thirds?
choices: Yes, because two pieces are the same size
No, thirds must be equal shares
questions.answer: No, thirds must be equal shares
questions.solution: Thirds are 3 EQUAL shares. These pieces are not all the same size, so they are not thirds.

solve.answer: No, thirds must be equal shares

questions.skill: A whole is made of its shares
questions.stem: Ruth says 4 fourths make a whole. Sam says 3 fourths make a whole. Who is right?
questions.solution: A whole cut into fourths has 4 fourths, so 4 fourths make the whole. 3 fourths is not all of it.

solve.work: 4 fourths make a whole; 3 fourths do not. Only Ruth.

questions.skill: Shares left after some are used
questions.stem: Sue cuts a pie into thirds. She eats 1 third. How many thirds are left?
questions.solution: There are 3 thirds. 3 - 1 = 2 thirds are left.

questions.skill: Count shares across several wholes
questions.stem: Ned has 3 sandwiches that are the same size. He cuts each one into halves. How many halves does he have in all?
questions.solution: Each sandwich makes 2 halves. 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

questions.skill: Count shares across several wholes
questions.stem: A cook cuts 2 pizzas into thirds. How many thirds are there in all?
questions.solution: Each pizza has 3 thirds. 3 + 3 = 6.

questions.skill: Shares left after some are used
questions.stem: A rug is cut into fourths. Two fourths are red and the rest are blue. How many fourths are blue?
questions.solution: There are 4 fourths in all. 4 - 2 = 2 are blue.

questions.skill: More equal shares make smaller shares
questions.stem: One pizza is cut into halves. Another pizza of the same size is cut into thirds. How many more shares does the second pizza have than the first?
questions.solution: The first has 2 shares and the second has 3. 3 - 2 = 1 more.

questions.skill: Equal shares can have different shapes
questions.stem: Two rectangles are the same size. Mia cuts hers into 4 equal strips. Dev cuts his into 4 equal squares. Which is true?
choices: Only Mia cut hers into fourths
Only Dev cut his into fourths
Both are cut into fourths, even though the pieces have different shapes
Neither is cut into fourths, because the shapes are different
questions.answer: Both are cut into fourths, even though the pieces have different shapes
questions.solution: Each rectangle is cut into 4 equal shares, so each piece is a fourth. Equal shares can have different shapes.

solve.answer: Both are cut into fourths, even though the pieces have different shapes
solve.work: Both cut same-size rectangles into 4 equal pieces, so both are fourths; shapes may differ.

questions.skill: More equal shares make smaller shares
questions.stem: Same-size pizzas are cut into halves, thirds and fourths. Which list goes from the biggest share to the smallest?
choices: A fourth, a third, a half
A half, a third, a fourth
A third, a half, a fourth
A half, a fourth, a third
questions.answer: A half, a third, a fourth
questions.solution: The fewer the shares, the bigger each one. Halves are biggest, then thirds, then fourths.

solve.answer: A half, a third, a fourth

questions.skill: Equal shares can have different shapes
questions.stem: Ava cuts a square sheet of paper straight down the middle into 2 pieces. Ben cuts a same-size square sheet from one corner to the opposite corner into 2 pieces. In each sheet, the 2 pieces are the same size. What is true?
choices: Neither makes halves, because the shapes are different
Both make halves, but the shapes of the halves are different
questions.answer: Both make halves, but the shapes of the halves are different
questions.solution: Each sheet is cut into 2 equal shares, so each piece is a half. Ava gets rectangles and Ben gets triangles. Equal shares can have different shapes.

solve.answer: Both make halves, but the shapes of the halves are different
solve.work: Both cut into 2 equal-size pieces (rectangles vs triangles): both halves, different shapes.

questions.skill: Name equal shares as halves, thirds or fourths
questions.stem: A pizza is cut into 3 equal shares. Sara eats 1 share. What is the part of the pizza that is left?
questions.solution: 3 thirds in all. 1 is eaten, so 3 - 1 = 2 thirds are left.

questions.skill: More equal shares make smaller shares
questions.stem: Hana says a third of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza. Which reason is right?
choices: More equal shares means each share is bigger
Fewer equal shares means each share is smaller
More equal shares means each share is smaller
Thirds always have a different shape than halves
questions.answer: More equal shares means each share is smaller
questions.solution: A pizza cut into 3 equal shares has smaller shares than one cut into 2. So a third is smaller than a half.

solve.answer: More equal shares means each share is smaller
solve.work: A third is smaller because more equal shares means each share is smaller.

questions.skill: Count shares across several wholes
questions.stem: A baker cuts 4 pies into thirds. How many thirds does the baker have?
questions.solution: Each pie has 3 thirds. 4 pies make 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 thirds.

questions.skill: Count shares across several wholes
questions.stem: Mr. Lee has 6 cakes of the same size. He cuts each cake into fourths. How many fourths does he have?
questions.solution: Each cake has 4 fourths. 6 cakes make 6 groups of 4: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 24.

questions.skill: Find how many wholes from the shares
questions.stem: Mia cut paper circles into thirds and got 15 thirds in all. How many circles did she cut?
questions.solution: Each circle makes 3 thirds. Count by 3s: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. That is 5 circles.

questions.skill: Count shares across several wholes
questions.stem: Tom cuts 2 pizzas into halves and 2 pizzas into fourths. How many shares are there in all?
questions.solution: The two pizzas cut into halves make 2 + 2 = 4 shares. The two cut into fourths make 4 + 4 = 8 shares. 4 + 8 = 12.

questions.skill: Count shares across several wholes
questions.stem: Grace has 3 pizzas cut into halves, 1 pizza cut into thirds and 1 pizza cut into fourths. How many shares are there in all?
questions.solution: The 3 pizzas cut into halves have 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 shares. Add 3 thirds and 4 fourths: 6 + 3 + 4 = 13.
